title: At what point do you give up on a game project?
author: BJGG69
selftext: I ran a small playtest and the feedback is pretty terrible, seems like the rework would require the same amount of effort as building a new game. Do I give up and move on to other ideas or do I go back to the drawing board and invest the effort needed to make the game better?

comments.author: CharacterTension2896
comments.body: How did you run the play test, and where. May be looking at the wrong audience

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: Asked a few classmates for feedback with 3 questions (Is it fun? Would you share it? What would you fix?). First two were No, the last one was mostly about the game needing an overhaul.

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: thats an incredibly small (and maybe weirdly biased against you) sample size.  maybe post it here so we can try?

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body:
It is a rather silly game, but I have reworked the experience and the visuals as per the initial round of feedback. Here is a link: [https://combos.game/play/ff335736bac2404c2d14878505702b08?share\_platform=web&share\_source=creator\_header](https://combos.game/play/ff335736bac2404c2d14878505702b08?share_platform=web&share_source=creator_header)

Would appreciate any feedback you've got

comments.author: chrismjf
comments.body: Just make what you enjoy or you’ll burn out and have nothing to show for it

comments.author: Baraga91
comments.body:
That all depends on you :)

The big quesiton for any core game concept is: is it fun? 

And if it is: "how much of the bells and whistles can I remove before it stops being fun?"

If it's a fun game, even when you basically play it on 40 year old 8 bit system, you can decide for yourself how much of your time you're willing to sink into fixing the issues or rebuilding.

Game development is like writing: you have to be willing to kill your darlings and start over.

comments.author: JohnSnowHenry
comments.body: I don’t. Even of it’s trash it’s still finalized :)

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: I like that attitude, maybe I should borrow this approach in this instance

comments.author: xloob
comments.body: Whenever I have an even better more exciting idea!

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: I feel like there is a huge gap between the idea in my head and the actual game after the first execution. And I can't tell if the original idea was a terrible one or the execution was a pile of manure.

comments.author: Confident-Emu-3150
comments.body:
A few things. First, it's a playtest, it's what it's for. A small audience, which might not be representative, gives you their opinion. Feedback can be positive... Or not. There are some game genres you dislike and will never like, and it's okay. Always keep that in mind.

With that being said, I think it's always good to push an experience as far as possible. The core question is "why isn't this working on this audience", why aren't they having fun, and how do you improve that. It doesn't mean starting from scratch again. Maybe it's not engaging enough, maybe it's not rewarding enough, maybe the gameplay is too slow, etc etc. You might have the right ideas, maybe you need a few more game mechanics, or maybe it's the implementation.

comments.author: DarkTemplar_
comments.body:
there are so many factors influencing this decision

Was it the actual target group?  
Was the keyloop of the game the problem or the things around  
Was the Keyloop understandable so the people understood what was asked from them?  
What is your goal? Want to do build a game you enjoy or you can sell or play with friends?

comments.author: ReleasePossible2731
comments.body: It depends on the you :) if you still feel strongly about this game and are willing to put more effort - absolutely go ahead, get back to the drawing board and rebuild. If you don’t like the concept anymore - drop it. Playtest are exactly for what you got - feedback. Take it with a pinch of salt - I found that people willing to playtest also tend to share feedback to improve more willingly than saying something nice, even if they really enjoyed it. That being said, you don’t need nice. You need ppl having fun with what you’ve built. You can also count this one as a complete project and move on to a ‘new’ one - that’s a complete rebuild. Sometimes it’s easier to wrap things up and restart fresh, as in to reset the stopwatch in your head on how much time the project has taken

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body:
>people willing to playtest also tend to share feedback to improve more willingly than saying something nice

That's so accurate - guess the feedback itself to overhaul could be a positive sign in itself, given that the people still saw potential there, if executed properly

comments.author: BansheeTheGame
comments.body: Before deciding to restart or move on, I’d validate the feedback itself. Were these the players you’re building for, and did multiple people identify the same problems? Ignore the impossible wish-list items and prioritize the changes that support the game’s core. Don’t lose heart—most big reworks become manageable when broken into small steps.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: Keep a goal in mind, and stay realistic if you can achieve it. When something falls apart completely, it can be hard to see what you can recover vs start fresh. The 80%/20% rule comes in fast. The last 20% of your game could take as long or longer than the first 80%. This can feel like slowing down but is normal. What is important is can you take that list of things and apply them one at a time and reach a new level?

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: If you start from scratch, maybe your next playtest will also have terrible feedback and you're back to starting again. At some point you have to respond to the feedback and improve on the game. But it depends on the type of feedback - do you have a vision for the game that the audience isn't getting yet and it needs more work toward selling the concept? Is the core of the game just bad and nobody is enjoying it? You just have to play it by ear and see if you believe in the idea enough to keep working at it
